summary:
Red Planet Outpost is a browser game where kids aged 7–12 look after a four-person base in Jezero Crater on Mars. There’s never enough power for everything, so players decide what to switch on: the air maker, grow lights for the greenhouse, the science lab, the radio dish or the storm shelter. Each of the five sols brings a new problem: the long cold night, a satellite that only passes twice a day, a dust storm, a broken air maker and a solar storm. Eight short lab games let players earn extra science, and tapping the Sun, Earth, Phobos or a dust devil turns up hidden facts.

The numbers come from real NASA missions: radiation measured by Curiosity, temperatures from Perseverance’s weather station, Opportunity’s power loss in the 2018 dust storm, and NASA’s life-support figures. Every number shows its source in the game. It runs in any browser with no sign-up, so it’s easy for kids and classrooms to play. Kids leave knowing something true about life on Mars: every choice costs something, and good planning keeps the crew alive.
details:
What it does
Red Planet Outpost is a browser game where kids aged 7–12 run a small base for four astronauts in Jezero Crater on Mars. The solar panels only make power during the day, and there’s never enough for everything. So players keep deciding what to switch on: the air maker, the greenhouse grow lights, the science lab, the radio dish or the storm shelter. Every choice costs something. Run the lab all afternoon and there may not be enough battery to keep the heaters going overnight. Skip the satellite pass and your science never reaches Earth.

How it works
The game has five sols (Mars days), and each one adds a new problem:

  1. The long cold night: living on the battery after sunset.
  2. The radio dish: a satellite that passes only twice a sol.
  3. A dust storm: solar power drops to a third.
  4. A broken air maker: players either fix it themselves (costs power, the lab stops) or wait for Earth’s answer (a real message delay).
  5. A solar storm: the crew has to shelter.

Players tap a building and a crew member walks out to switch it. The battery forecast shows whether power will last until sunrise. When the lab is on, it collects rock samples that unlock eight short science games, such as sorting rocks, focusing a microscope or driving a rover around soft sand. They get harder as the sol goes on, and failing costs points. Tapping the Sun, Earth, Phobos or a dust devil turns up hidden facts.

Real NASA data
The numbers come from real missions:

  • Radiation measured by Curiosity’s RAD detector, including the 20 May 2024 solar storm.
  • Day and night temperatures from Perseverance’s MEDA weather station.
  • How dust cut Opportunity’s solar power in 2018.
  • NASA’s figure for how much oxygen an astronaut breathes.
  • MOXIE’s oxygen results.

The Earth–Mars message delay is calculated for the day you play, from JPL’s planet orbit data. A “Where the numbers come from” page labels every number as real, based on real data, made up for gameplay, or calculated, with its source.

Benefits and impact
Kids don’t just read that Mars is hard to live on. They feel it, because they make the same trade-offs mission planners do. We hope players come away understanding that good planning, not luck, keeps a crew alive. The game also works for classrooms: it’s free, needs no sign-up and runs on laptops, tablets and phones.

What makes it creative
Each level is built around one real trade-off rather than a list of facts. The science counter shows points piling up in the lab, then moving to Earth during a satellite pass. The minigames turn real rover science into quick challenges, and the hidden facts reward kids who explore.

What we considered

  • Audience: plain words for ages 7–12, with terms like “sol” explained in the game.
  • Not overwhelming players: only a few systems at once, with a guide on the first sol.
  • Failure as a lesson: a failed sol explains what went wrong and lets you try again.
  • Fairness: every goal was checked with computer runs, so each sol can be won on both difficulty levels.
  • Honesty: the data is archived, not live, and the game says so.

We made use of of NASA data fields in our projects. Below is the list of how each data filed is used in our game.

  • Curiosity RAD pages: RAD measures radiation on Mars and during the trip there. The second article reports the 20 May 2024 storm reading the game uses on Sol 5.
  • MEDA page: MEDA is Perseverance’s weather station, measuring temperature, wind, pressure and humidity. It’s where the game’s temperatures come from.
  • Opportunity pages: dust in the air is measured as “tau”. The last tau Opportunity recorded was 10.8, against about 0.5 on a normal day. That’s what the dust storm on Sol 3 is shaped on.
  • MOXIE data: MOXIE made 122 grams of oxygen in total, up to 12 grams an hour. Those are the numbers in the oxygen-maker game.
  • JPL page: gives the planet positions the game uses to work out today’s Earth–Mars message delay.

Tools
HTML, CSS and JavaScript, in a single web page with hand-drawn SVG graphics. It needs no downloads or plugins. An AI assistant (Claude by Anthropic) helped write and test the code and draft text. The game idea, design decisions and testing direction came from our team.
